tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetes > Definition, classification and treatment targets
tables.caption: Diabetes mellitus: definition, classification and treatment targets

body.t: Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic condition in which the pancreas no longer produces enough insulin (impaired insulin secretion) or cells stop responding to the insulin that is produced (insulin resistance), resulting in increased blood glucose.

1. Type 1 diabetes: due to autoimmune b-cell destruction, usually leading to absolute insulin deficiency, including latent autoimmune diabetes of adulthood. 2. Type 2 diabetes: due to a progressive loss of b-cell insulin secretion, frequently on the background of insulin resistance.

Monogenic diabetes syndromes (neonatal diabetes; maturity-onset diabetes of the young). Diseases of the exocrine pancreas (such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatitis). Drug- or chemical-induced diabetes: glucocorticoid use, treatment of HIV/AIDS, or after organ transplantation. Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): diabetes diagnosed in the second or third trimester of pregnancy that was not clearly overt diabetes before gestation.
HbA1c <7% for most adults. HbA1c <6.5% for type 1 diabetes without hypoglycaemia. HbA1c <8% for people with frequent hypoglycaemia, limited life expectancy, or cardiovascular complications.
All clients on treatment should aim for a glycaemia (random or fasting) ranging 5-10 mmol/L.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment
tables.caption: Type 2 diabetes pharmacological treatment (flowchart, by HbA1c)
tables.content:
Newly diagnosed type 2 DM patient: check HbA1c. Health promotion for all (disease, medication adherence, nutrition, behaviour), individual and group.

By HbA1c at diagnosis:
- HbA1c <7%: lifestyle modification; recheck HbA1c in 6 months.
- HbA1c 7-8% (printed '<7%-8%'): start metformin [note 1]: 1. 500 mg OD; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase dose every 3 months until at goal or maximum tolerated dose.
- HbA1c 8-9.9% (printed '<8%-9.9%'): consider dual therapy: 1. start metformin 500 mg OD and titrate every 2 weeks to a maximum of 2 g if tolerated; 2. add a second drug (sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors).
- HbA1c >10%: consider insulin: consider starting the patient on insulin therapy alone or in combination with metformin (consult physician). Start at low-dose insulin and increase until target reached.

Follow-up after lifestyle modification or metformin:
- HbA1c <7%: 1. continue current medication; 2. recheck HbA1c in 6 months; 3. fasting blood glucose every 3 months.
- HbA1c >7%: 1. add a second OGLA, e.g. sulfonylurea, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, GLP-1 agonists or SGLT-2 inhibitors; 2. recheck HbA1c in 3 months; 3. increase the dose of the second agent until glycaemic target reached, or maximum dose. If HbA1c remains >8%, review with physician and consider referral to the diabetes clinic for insulin management.

T2DM diagnosis criteria: 1. FPG > 7.0 mmol/L; 2. random glucose > 11.1 mmol/L; 3. need two positive tests, one must be FBG.
For older patients, it is reasonable to set the HbA1c goal at < 8%.

[note 1] Caution: metformin use in patients with reduced kidney function: 1. do not start new patients on metformin if CrCl < 45 ml/min; 2. continue metformin if already on it and CrCl is 30-45 ml/min, but repeat CrCl in 6 months; 3. stop metformin if CrCl < 30 ml/min.

The diagnosis criteria here (FPG > 7.0, two positive tests) differ slightly from the diagnosis box on p.22 (FPG ≥ 7.0, HbA1c ≥ 6.5%).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Oral agents used in the management of type 2 diabetes
tables.caption: Oral agents used in the management of type 2 diabetes: doses, frequency, side effects and contraindications

body.section: A. Sulphonylureas. Mechanism of action: stimulate the pancreas to release insulin (regardless of time and glucose levels)

body.t: Caution in liver and renal disease
Pregnancy; caution in liver and renal disease
Pregnancy; caution in liver and renal disease

body.section: B. Biguanide. Mechanism of action: (i) reduce glucose production in liver; (ii) cause (mild) reduction in peripheral insulin resistance

body.t: Abdominal pain, nausea, loose bowel motions, lactic acidosis; vitamin B12 deficiency with prolonged use
Renal failure, GFR <30 ml/min; heart failure stage 3 or 4; liver failure

body.section: C. Thiazolidinediones. Mechanism of action: (i) improved insulin sensitivity in muscle, adipose tissue and liver; (ii) reduce glucose output from liver; (iii) change fat distribution by decreasing visceral fat and increasing peripheral fat

body.t: Liver impairment, fluid retention, weight gain, dilutional anemia, osteoporosis
Heart failure and liver failure; pregnancy; bone fractures

body.section: D. Meglitinides. Mechanism of action: stimulate pancreas to release more insulin (possibly related to blood glucose level)

body.t: Liver impairment, fluid retention, weight gain, dilutional anemia

body.section: E. Alpha glucosidase inhibitors. Mechanism of action: slow digestion of complex sugars (sucrose and starch), delaying absorption and the post-meal rise in blood glucose
F. DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins). Mechanism of action: improve pancreatic islet glucose sensing, increasing glucose-mediated insulin secretion and suppressing glucagon secretion

body.t: Urticaria, angioedema, and immune mediated dermatologic effects. Acute pancreatitis. Risk of hypoglycemia
Pancreatitis; allergy, pregnancy, lactation; caution with heart failure (saxagliptin)

body.section: G. SGLT-2 inhibitors. Mechanism of action: suppress renal glucose reabsorption by blocking the sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 (SGLT-2), increasing urinary glucose excretion

body.t: Polyurea, UTI, DKA, genital candidiasis, hypotension
Renal failure (action dependent on normal GFR), or sensitivity to active ingredients or its excipients

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Outpatient > Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes
tables.caption: Pharmacotherapy progression in type 2 diabetes (monotherapy to triple therapy and insulin)

body.t: Metformin is the drug of first choice at diagnosis.

Continue until contraindicated or not tolerated. If metformin is contraindicated or not tolerated, use gliclazide. For patients with established cardiovascular disease intolerant to metformin, consider SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1RA (under specialist care).
Consider if the patient has symptomatic hyperglycaemia and HbA1c >9% at diagnosis. Review gliclazide continuation once metformin dose and lifestyle interventions are optimized.
Add a second agent if target not achieved with monotherapy

Options to add: gliclazide, DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, or SGLT2 inhibitor. Consider comorbidities, ability to access medicines, and properties of each drug. Fixed-dose combinations (e.g., DPP-4 inhibitor + metformin) may offer compliance and cost advantages.
Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent

Consider if HbA1c is above individualized target (typically <7% for most) with two oral agents. Injectable options: GLP-1RA or basal insulin. Do NOT combine: GLP-1RA with DPP-4 inhibitor; GLP-1RA with SGLT2 inhibitor; pioglitazone with insulin.
Add a third oral agent or an injectable agent.
For patients on three oral agents who are still not at target. Other oral agents can be stopped upon initiation of premix insulin.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Indications and timing for insulin
tables.caption: Insulin therapy in type 2 diabetes: indications, when to initiate, and good practice

body.t: Poor glycaemic control: HbA1c still [above target] despite previous attempts to improve with lifestyle modification and maximum oral therapy. Patient is symptomatic (weight loss, polyuria, polydipsia, recurrent infections). Steroid-induced diabetes. Patient unable to tolerate or has contraindication to OGLAs. Gestational diabetes or diabetes in pregnancy not controlled on OGLAs. Painful neuropathy. Foot ulceration and infection.

As soon as there is evidence of sub-optimal glycaemic control. After reviewing the patient's ability to change their lifestyle and medication concordance. Following a full discussion with the patient that includes identifying barriers to insulin initiation, e.g. occupational issues, fear of weight gain, fear of hypoglycaemia and fear of injections.

Insulin initiation should be part of a structured educational programme for the patient, and competent health care staff should have sufficient time for initiation and follow-up until glycaemic control is optimized. The decision to start insulin should be made in partnership with the person, and the choice of regimen should cater for individual needs. The person initiating insulin should be trained and competent to do so in line with the national guidelines, and should consult with the physician/diabetologist. Ensure educational materials and support literature are available for the patient starting insulin. Patients requiring insulin prior to pregnancy should be referred to the gynaecologist.

tables.context_before: Diabetes is a progressive condition, and many patients with type 2 diabetes eventually require and benefit from insulin therapy.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy in Type 2 Diabetes > Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM
tables.caption: Stepwise approach to insulin initiation in type 2 DM (flowchart)
tables.content:
Steps run from 1 injection (more flexible, lower patient complexity) to 3+ injections (less flexible, high complexity).

Step 1 - Basal insulin (usually with metformin), 1 injection:
  Start: 10 units per day, or 0.1 to 0.2 units per kg per day.
  Adjust: 10% to 15%, or 2 to 4 units, once or twice weekly to reach fasting BG target.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 4 units or 10% to 20%.

If not controlled after fasting BG target is reached (or if dose > 0.5 units per kg per day), treat postprandial glucose excursions with mealtime insulin (consider an initial glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonist trial). Two options (2 injections, moderate complexity):

Option A - Add 1 rapid-acting insulin injection before the largest meal:
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose; if A1C <8%, consider decreasing basal insulin by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Option B - Change to premixed insulin twice daily:
  Start: divide current basal dose into 2/3 a.m. and 1/3 p.m., or into 1/2 a.m. and 1/2 p.m.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.
  If not controlled: consider basal-bolus (Step 3).

Step 3 - Add 2 or more rapid-acting insulin injections before the largest meals (basal-bolus, 3+ injections, high complexity):
  Start: 4 units, 0.1 units per kg, or 10% of basal dose per meal; if A1C < 8%, consider decreasing basal dose by the same amount.
  Adjust: increase dose by 1 to 2 units or 10% to 15% once or twice weekly until SMBG target is reached.
  For hypoglycaemia: determine and address cause; decrease dose by 2 to 4 units or 10% to 20%.

NB: for clients already on a single injectable agent, e.g. basal insulin, consider escalation to any of: 1. combination basal insulin and GLP-1RA therapy; 2. premix (twice daily) insulin; 3. basal-plus insulin therapy (adding one or more prandial doses of insulin to basal insulin). For all three options, metformin should be retained; consider stopping the other oral agents to reduce the cost and complexity of the regimen.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 1 Diabetes > Signs and symptoms of type 1 diabetes
tables.caption: Type 1 diabetes: signs and symptoms by severity (early, severe without loss of consciousness, severe with coma)

body.t: Polyuria; polydipsia; polyphagia; weight loss and/or poor weight gain; enuresis/nocturia; fatigue; blurred vision; perineal candidiasis (esp. prepubertal girls); inability and decreasing performance at school

Hyperglycaemia (high blood sugar); dehydration due to fluid loss; cellular energy deficit; catabolism (breakdown of fat/muscle); polyuria (excessive night-time urination); lack of energy utilization; osmotic changes in the eye lens; localized fungal infection due to glucose in urine; general malaise/fatigue/frequent bathroom breaks
Polyuria with severe dehydration; polydipsia; fast deep breathing (hyperventilation); presence of fruity (sweet) breath

Uncontrolled hyperglycaemia and significant fluid loss; severe dehydration; compensatory mechanism for metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing); diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): presence of acetone/ketones
Severe hyperglycaemia which may progress to neurological compromise, seizures, and coma
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)

source_flags: The old chunks repeated the premixed-insulin table here; the early and severe-without-coma rows were missing.
tables.context_before: All children and adolescents with type 1 diabetes require insulin. Poorly controlled type 1 diabetes increases the risk of stunted growth and diabetes complications, including diabetic ketoacidosis.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Type 1 Diabetes > Diagnosis of T1DM
tables.caption: Diagnosis of type 1 diabetes (T1DM)
tables.content:
Three stages, shown as three boxes:
1. Symptoms (loss of weight, polyuria, polydipsia, ...): increased risk of diabetes. Suspect diabetes.
2. Symptoms + glucose criteria: in case of abnormal plasma glucose values, experts suggest getting an HbA1c as a useful baseline. Diabetes is confirmed by: fasting plasma glucose ≥7.0 mmol/L (≥126 mg/dl); random plasma glucose ≥11.1 mmol/L (≥200 mg/dl); HbA1c ≥ 6.5%. Immune-mediated diabetes: presence of autoimmune markers.
3. Immune-mediated diabetes (in tertiary care): presence of autoimmune markers: islet cell autoantibodies and autoantibodies to GAD (GAD65), insulin, the tyrosine phosphatases IA-2 and IA-2β, and ZnT8.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Insulin Therapy for Type 1 Diabetes > Insulin regimens > Insulin dosage regimens
tables.caption: Insulin dosage regimens for type 1 diabetes: share of total daily dose by meal (basal-bolus, split-mixed, three and two injections)

body.t: 20% of total daily dose (if able to count carbohydrates: give 1 unit per 15 g)
Intermediate acting (ideally this ought to be a basal insulin acting over 24 hours)
Short acting insulin (30% of morning dose) + intermediate acting (70% of morning dose)
Short acting insulin (1/3 of evening dose)

source_flags: Option 2 rows: 'Lunch: short acting insulin (1/3 of evening dose)' is printed as is; with 2/3 of the total in the morning the remaining 1/3 is the evening dose. Clinician to confirm the intended timing.
Basal-bolus 40% at night here vs '30-40%' in the text above.
tables.context_before: Basal-bolus regimen (preferred regimen): short acting insulin 15-30 minutes before a meal, or rapid acting insulin with main meals (e.g. breakfast, lunch and main evening meal); intermediate acting insulin before bed. Normally 30-40% of the total daily dose is given at bedtime as intermediate acting insulin; the remaining insulin is given before breakfast, lunch and the evening meal as short acting insulin. Short acting insulin is indicated in the child (especially <5 years of age) with erratic eating habits despite adequate education.
tables.table_note: OR three injections daily: a mixture of short and intermediate acting (premixed 70:30) insulin before breakfast; short acting insulin alone before an afternoon snack or main evening meal; intermediate acting insulin before bed (or variations). This requires that the caregiver is aware of three different insulin preparations and can differentiate between them. OR two injections daily: a mixture (premixed combination) of short and intermediate acting insulins before breakfast and the main evening meal. The total daily dose is divided so that 2/3 is given in the morning and 1/3 in the evening; each dose is split between intermediate-acting and short-acting insulin in a 70:30 ratio (pre-mixed). This regimen is less flexible, but easier to give administration instructions for.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Management of Diabetes Emergencies > Diagnosis, monitoring, resolution and subcutaneous insulin protocol
tables.caption: Management of diabetic emergencies (DKA and HHS): diagnosis, evaluation, monitoring, resolution, transition to SC insulin, alternative SC insulin protocol and formulas

body.t: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) are two of the most serious acute complications of diabetes. DKA is characterized by ketoacidosis and hyperglycemia, while HHS usually has more severe hyperglycemia without ketoacidosis.
Based on clinical evaluation and immediate bedside investigations. Features include polyuria, polydipsia, nausea, abdominal pain, fruity odor, confusion, Kussmaul breathing, dehydration.

Hyperglycemia: BG >13.9 mmol/L. Euglycemia <250 mg/dl (pregnancy, SGLT2 use). Ketonuria or ketonemia (>3 mmol/L): highly positive. Acidosis: pH <7.3, low HCO3- (printed ':<10 ≤ 15 mEq/L'). Anion gap: >12 (see formula).
Severe hyperglycemia: BG (printed '>600>1000 mg/dl 33.3 mmol/L'). Hyperosmolality: effective serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg (see formula). Neurologic signs: focal signs, obtundation, seizure, coma.

Vital signs, volume status (decreased skin turgor, dry axillae and oral mucosa, low JVP, tachycardia and hypotension), mental status. Immediately: serum blood glucose, urine ketones. Additional testing: FBC, electrolytes, FT, ABG. Evaluate for precipitating causes: septic screen (urinalysis, blood cultures), cardiac enzymes, ECG, CXR. Pregnancy test if indicated.

BG hourly. Urinary ketones and serum pH for DKA, and serum osmolality for HHS, 4-hourly. Electrolytes, primarily Na+ and K+, 4-hourly. Mental status: expect improvement with treatment if DKA or HHS are the causes; consider further evaluation if not improving. Input/output, hydration status; vital signs hourly.
BG < 15 mmol/L + 2 or more of: HCO3- ≥ 15 mEq/L; pH > 7.3; anion gap ≤ 12 mEq/L. Negative urine ketones if the above are not available (confirm with repeat in 1-2 hrs).
BG < [value missing in source]; improved mental status; effective osmolality ≤ 315 mOsm/kg.

Continue continuous IV for 1-2 hrs after long-acting insulin is started. 0.4-0.6 u/kg for insulin-naive patients. NPH/regular: based on inpatient DM protocol. Hold regular insulin if patient is not eating. May resume home regimen if previously on insulin.

This regimen is not well validated and is modified from other protocols; continuous IV is preferred as standard of care when available. If continuous infusion is not available, for mild/moderate DKA: initial IV bolus 0.1 IU/kg given intravenously; maintenance 0.1 IU/kg subcutaneous every 1-2 hours (start immediately following the bolus). When BG <250 mg/dL, reduce dose by 50%. Continue until resolution of DKA or HHS.

Calculated anion gap (>12 is elevated) = [Na+] − [Cl- + HCO3-]. Effective serum osmolality = 2x[Na+K] + urea + glucose (usually <330 mosmol/kg in DKA and > 350 mosmol/kg in HHS). Corrected serum sodium = [Na+] + 1.6 x [glucose (mg/dL) − 100]/100. Free water deficit = 0.6 x weight (kg) x [(Na+/140) − 1].

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 02 Immediate assessment (0-30 minutes)
tables.caption: 02 Immediate assessment of DKA/HHS (0-30 minutes): history, examination and urgent investigations

body.t: Airway, breathing, circulation, GCS. Precipitant: infection, omitted insulin, new DM, MI. Weight (actual or estimate) for fluid calculation. Catheterise if unconscious or anuric. Temperature, HR, BP, SpO2, RR. Kussmaul breathing, acetone breath (DKA). Neurological exam: focal deficits (HHS: thrombosis).

Capillary BGL + urine/blood ketones. Venous blood gas (VBG): pH, HCO3, lactate. U&E: Na+, K+, Cl-, urea, creatinine. FBC + differential, blood cultures if febrile. Urine MCS, CXR, ECG. HIV rapid test if status unknown. Calculated serum osmolality. Phosphate & magnesium if available.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 03 IV fluid resuscitation
tables.caption: 03 IV fluid resuscitation in DKA and HHS: regimen and rate by time

body.t: 0.9% NaCl: 1 L over 30-60 min. If SBP <90: 500 ml bolus, repeat once
0.9% NaCl: 1 L over 60 min. Slower if elderly/cardiac risk
0.9% NaCl: 500 ml/hr x2 hrs, then 250 ml/hr
0.9% NaCl 125-250 ml/hr; switch to 0.45% NaCl if corrected Na+ rising
0.45% NaCl 250 ml/hr once osmolality falling; correct deficit over 48 hrs
Switch to 0.9% NaCl + 5% dextrose OR 0.45% NaCl + 5% dextrose. Continue insulin: use dextrose to maintain target glucose range.

source_flags: The table note says correct the HHS deficit over 48-72 hours; the 4-12 hr row says over 48 hrs.
tables.context_before: Use 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) as first-line. Switch to 0.45% NaCl in HHS once glucose <20 mmol/L and osmolality falling. Add 5% dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L (DKA) or <15 mmol/L (HHS) to allow continued insulin without hypoglycaemia.
tables.table_note: WARNING: HHS: total deficit can be 8-15 litres. Correct over 48-72 hours. Rapid correction risks cerebral oedema and cardiac failure. Reassess every 2 hours. Target osmolality reduction 3-8 mOsm/kg/hr.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 06 Bicarbonate (DKA only, restricted use)
tables.caption: 06 Bicarbonate in DKA (restricted use): indication and regimen

body.t: pH <6.9 OR life-threatening hyperkalaemia (K+ >6.5 with ECG changes)
100 mmol (100 ml of 8.4%) NaHCO3 IV over 30 minutes. Add 20 mmol KCl to each infusion. Repeat VBG after 60 min; maximum 2 doses. Not recommended in HHS.

tables.context_before: WARNING: Do NOT routinely give bicarbonate in DKA: associated with paradoxical CNS acidosis, hypokalaemia, and worsened cerebral oedema.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 05 Insulin protocol
tables.caption: 05 Insulin protocol: DKA insulin infusion vs HHS insulin protocol

body.t:
1. Bolus (only if K+ ≥3.5): 0.1 unit/kg soluble (regular) insulin IV stat.
2. Continuous infusion: 0.1 unit/kg/hr soluble insulin IV. Dilute 50 units in 50 ml 0.9% NaCl (1 unit/ml) via syringe pump. If no pump: 50 units in 500 ml NS (0.1 unit/ml).
3. When glucose <14 mmol/L: reduce to 0.05 unit/kg/hr + add 5% dextrose to fluids. Target BGL 10-14 mmol/L until ketones clear / pH >7.3.

Step 1: fluids only for the first 1-2 hours, NO insulin. Glucose will fall with fluids alone; early insulin causes rapid osmolality drop and cerebral oedema.
Step 2: start insulin only when glucose is NOT falling >5 mmol/L/hr with fluids alone AND adequate fluid resuscitation is underway. Start at 0.05 unit/kg/hr (lower than DKA).
Step 3: target glucose reduction 3-4 mmol/L/hr. Target BGL 10-15 mmol/L. NEVER drop >5 mmol/L/hr.

tables.table_note: WARNING: Avoid SC insulin during IV fluid resuscitation: poor absorption due to vasoconstriction and dehydration. Do not stop insulin to treat hypoglycaemia: reduce rate and add dextrose.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 04 Potassium replacement protocol
tables.caption: 04 Potassium replacement protocol in DKA/HHS: action, KCl per litre and rate by serum K+

body.t: HOLD INSULIN: replace K+ urgently first. Recheck K+ in 1 hour before restarting insulin.
40 mmol KCl (central line only for >20 mmol/hr)
Normal: proceed with insulin. Monitor every 2 hours.
Hold K+ supplementation. Recheck in 2 hours.

source_flags: The >5.5 row gives 'No KCl' but a rate of '10-20 mmol/hr', as printed.
tables.table_note: Potassium safety rules: NEVER give undiluted KCl IV (fatal if bolused). Rates >20 mmol/hr require cardiac monitoring and central venous access. Initial K+ may appear high/normal despite total body depletion: watch closely as insulin drives K+ intracellularly. Hypokalaemia is the leading cause of preventable death in DKA.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 07 Monitoring schedule
tables.caption: 07 Monitoring schedule for DKA/HHS, and corrected sodium in hyperglycaemia

body.t: Capillary blood glucose, fluid balance (in/out), HR, BP, SpO2, RR
Serum K+, Na+, urea; venous blood gas; blood or urine ketones
Full U&E + creatinine; reassess fluid plan; neurological status
ECG if K+ abnormal or arrhythmia present
GCS: declining = cerebral oedema: STOP fluids and escalate
Target >0.5 ml/kg/hr. Catheterise if anuric or GCS <13

source_flags: The PDF prints the schedule as two side-by-side frequency/parameter pairs; listed as one column here.
'Every 2 hour' printed; written 'Every 2 hours'.
tables.table_note: Corrected sodium in hyperglycaemia: measured Na+ is falsely low in hyperglycaemia. Add 1.6 mmol/L to measured Na+ for every 5.5 mmol/L glucose above 5.5 mmol/L. If corrected Na+ is rising despite resuscitation, switch to 0.45% NaCl. Persistent hypernatraemia in HHS suggests under-resuscitation.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Algorithm for management of DKA and HHS > 08 Resolution criteria and transition to SC insulin
tables.caption: 08 Resolution criteria for DKA and HHS, and 3-step transition to subcutaneous insulin

body.t: Blood glucose <14 mmol/L; venous pH >7.3; HCO3- >15 mmol/L; ketonaemia <0.6 mmol/L (or ketonuria <1+); patient able to eat and drink.
Serum osmolality <310 mOsm/kg; blood glucose <15 mmol/L; clinically well, normal GCS; patient eating and drinking; no further vomiting.
Give SC insulin dose at mealtime. Ensure patient has eaten before injecting.
Continue IV insulin infusion for at least 30-60 minutes AFTER SC injection to avoid gap.
Known DM: resume pre-admission regimen. New DM: start basal-bolus 0.5 unit/kg/day (50% basal, 50% bolus divided over 3 meals).

source_flags: Resolution criteria here (BG <14 mmol/L, pH >7.3, HCO3- >15, all required) differ from the management box on p.34 (BG <15 mmol/L + 2 or more criteria). Clinician to confirm which applies.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Complications to anticipate and manage
tables.caption: DKA/HHS complications to anticipate: recognition and management, and when to escalate

body.t: Declining GCS, headache, bradycardia after initial improvement
Reduce fluids; mannitol 0.5-1 g/kg IV; urgent transfer to higher level
Commonest preventable death. ECG: U waves, ST depression, QT prolongation
Check K+ every 2 hrs, replace aggressively per protocol (section 04)
Glucose falling too rapidly or <4 mmol/L
Add dextrose to fluids; NEVER stop insulin: reduce rate instead
Non-anion gap acidosis despite DKA treatment, large NS volumes given
Switch to balanced crystalloid (Ringer's lactate) if available; reduce NS
High risk in HHS: may be clinically silent
LMWH prophylaxis: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (no contraindication). TED stockings
Crackles on auscultation, SpO2 falling, worsening dyspnoea
Reduce fluid rate; furosemide if fluid overloaded; CXR; oxygen
Urine output <0.5 ml/kg/hr persisting after resuscitation
Ensure adequate fluids; avoid nephrotoxins; urgent nephrology review if severe
Fever, leukocytosis, clinical signs of source
Empirical antibiotics: co-amoxiclav or ceftriaxone; cultures before antibiotics; check HIV

tables.table_note: WARNING: ESCALATE TO HIGHER LEVEL OF CARE if GCS <13, pH <7.0, K+ <2.5 or >7.0, SBP <80 not responding to fluids, declining despite 4 hours of treatment, suspected cerebral oedema, pregnancy with DKA, or need for ICU monitoring. Contact Mbabane Government Hospital or Raleigh Fitkin Memorial Hospital referral pathway.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 2: Endocrinology > Diabetic Emergencies > Discharge criteria and patient education
tables.caption: Discharge criteria after DKA/HHS and discharge education checklist

body.t: Medically stable ≥24 hours on SC insulin. Eating and drinking normally. Precipitating cause identified and treated. Blood glucose consistently 4-10 mmol/L pre-meal. Diabetes education completed. Follow-up appointment arranged.

Sick day rules: never stop insulin during illness. When to seek emergency care (glucose, ketones, vomiting). Insulin injection technique and site rotation. Blood glucose monitoring targets and timing. Dietary counselling by dietitian. Prescription: insulin + glucometer + test strips. Outpatient follow-up: 1 week, then 4-6 weekly.
